tagline: Old road alignments and a railway corridor shape the coastal drive.
intro: The Lemon Bay/Myakka Trail is a 47-mile scenic highway on Florida’s southwestern coast, designated April 9, 2008. Florida Scenic Highways highlights its barrier islands, Manasota Key beaches, Myakka State Forest trails and Olde Englewood Village Historic District. SR 776, the 25-mile highway between South Venice and Murdock, was widened to four lanes in the 1990s and early 2000s.

Part of the journey once belonged to the Tamiami Trail: Old Englewood Road, Dearborn Street and River Road carried an early alignment through Englewood. The Myakka crossing began as a wooden bridge beside the railway in 1928, extending the road northeast from McCall to the developing town of El Jobean. By the 1930s, that trail had shifted north, bypassing town. Farther east, the railway beside El Jobean Road was abandoned in 1981; road widening used its former right of way in the 1990s.

Start at US 41 in South Venice and follow SR 776 southwest through Woodmere into Englewood. Beach Road branches across Lemon Bay to Manasota Key. Back on SR 776, the route turns east, passes north of Rotonda West, then bends northeast across the Myakka River into El Jobean. Continue through Port Charlotte to the return to US 41 at Murdock.

moments.title: Englewood
moments.text: Dearborn, Harvard and Yale carry names borrowed from Chicago streets. The three brothers who developed Englewood named it for their hometown of Englewood, Chicago; the Florida town’s original plat was filed in August 1896. That was a difficult time for local citrus. Freezes in 1894, 1895 and 1896 destroyed many orange plants, and the 1897 Manatee County General Directory listed fish as Englewood’s chief product. Dearborn Street also belonged to an early Tamiami Trail alignment, before the highway shifted north and bypassed Englewood by the 1930s. West Dearborn Street now holds the town’s small shopping district.

moments.title: Manasota Key
moments.text: Beach Road crosses Lemon Bay from Englewood to Manasota Key, with the Gulf of Mexico along the key’s western edge. The 11-mile peninsula became a barrier island through construction of the Gulf Intracoastal Waterway. Its name came from the Manasota Lumber Company, which operated a Woodmere sawmill from 1918 to 1923. Manasota combines manatee and Sarasota. At the southern end, Stump Pass connects the bay with the Gulf and separates Manasota Key from Don Pedro Island. Englewood Beach occupies the Charlotte County portion; farther along the peninsula, Manasota Beach lies in Sarasota County.

moments.title: El Jobean
moments.text: El Jobean sits off SR 776 on the Myakka River’s northern bank. Its name rearranges the letters of Joel Bean, the developer who laid out the town in the 1920s. A post office operated here from 1924 until 1964. In 1928, a wooden bridge beside the railway brought the road across the Myakka to El Jobean. The wooden crossing was replaced by a concrete bridge in 1959; a second bridge followed in 2001. The two concrete bridges divide traffic by direction: the 2001 span carries westbound vehicles, while eastbound traffic uses the 1959 bridge.
